feed.title: BIP Draft Post-Quantum Address Format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65

entry.title: BIP Draft Post-Quantum Address Format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65
entry.summary:
A proposal has been introduced for a new Bitcoin address format, designated as bc1z, which leverages ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) post-quantum digital signatures. This format builds upon the security model of existing SegWit addresses by committing to a SHA-256 hash of the public key, with the full public key revealed only during the spend operation within the transaction witness. The intention is to provide resistance against attacks from quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptographic standards such as ECDSA and Schnorr, both of which are vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm. At present, a significant portion of Bitcoin—approximately 6.9 million BTC, valued at around $586 billion—is held in addresses where public keys have already been exposed on-chain, making them susceptible to future quantum threats.
The technical design specifies an address format structured as bc1z followed by a witness version (0x02) and a 32-byte SHA-256 commitment. When spending from these addresses, the witness includes an ML-DSA signature, sized at 3,309 bytes, and an ML-DSA public key, sized at 1,952 bytes. Compatibility with the existing network is achieved through a soft fork, allowing older nodes to interpret bc1z outputs as anyone-can-spend, due to the use of a witness version greater than one. A reference implementation is available as a Python library, featuring key management, signing, verification, migration support, and a monitoring tool for quantum vulnerabilities. Additionally, there is a prototype for aggregating ML-DSA signatures using SNARKs, enabling compression of approximately 33KB of individual signatures down to about 2KB when aggregating ten signatures.
Further information, including the draft specification, can be found in the [btc-safe repository](https://github.com/Zaenus/btc-safe), specifically under docs/bip/0001-pq-address-format.md. The project invites community feedback on several aspects: the design of the address format, the selection of ML-DSA-65 parameters balancing security and signature size, deployment strategies via a soft fork, approaches for migrating existing UTXOs, and the overall urgency of adopting quantum-resistant solutions prior to the advent of cryptographically relevant quantum computers. Input from the broader development community will inform the evolution of this proposal.
